name: Sunscreen-maxxing

card.summary: Daily SPF and strict reapplication to limit UV exposure and the skin ageing attributed to it.
card.note: Allergic reactions possible; ingredient rules differ by country.

quick.overview:
Sunscreen-maxxing means wearing sunscreen daily and reapplying, mainly to prevent sun-driven skin ageing: lines, dark spots, laxity and visible blood vessels.

A randomised Australian trial reported smoother skin after 4.5 years of daily broad-spectrum use compared with usual habits, and dermatology bodies recommend daily broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher.
quick.how: Practitioners choose a broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher product, apply it to the face and exposed skin every morning, and reapply about every two hours when outdoors or after swimming or sweating, often alongside hats and sunglasses.
quick.risks: Reported issues include allergic contact dermatitis and, in some aerosols, benzene contamination leading to recalls. Typical use is not usually linked to vitamin D deficiency. Studies find many people apply too little.

lead: Sunscreen-maxxing is the looksmaxxing term for strict daily sunscreen use, with regular reapplication, to limit ultraviolet exposure and the skin ageing attributed to it. Its appeal for appearance is that chronic UV exposure drives wrinkles, laxity, freckles, dark spots and visible blood vessels, so blocking UV is a way to keep skin smoother, more even and younger-looking for longer.[1][2]

Sunscreens are rated by sun protection factor (SPF), introduced by Franz Greiter in 1974, which mainly reflects protection against UVB.[2] Broad-spectrum products also protect against UVA, which penetrates deeper and damages collagen and elastin.[1][2] The American Academy of Dermatology advises a broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen of SPF 30 or higher, reapplied about every two hours outdoors, and the FDA gives similar label-based guidance.[3][4] Wikipedia's article on photoageing describes sun protection as the most effective primary prevention.[1]

A 2013 Australian study of about 900 people reported that those who applied broad-spectrum sunscreen daily for four and a half years had smoother, more resilient skin than those who used it as they chose.[2]

chain: Daily broad-spectrum SPF blocks UVA and UVB
Less collagen breakdown and less melanin stimulation
Fewer lines, spots and redness over the years
angle.text: Sunscreen reduces the UV that causes wrinkling, laxity and dark spots, so the skin keeps a smoother, more even look. Sunscreen-maxxers apply it every day and reapply through the day to maintain that protection.

infobox: Sunscreen (nonprescription drug in the US; cosmetic in the EU)[2][4]

paras: Practitioners apply sunscreen every day, including on cloudy days, and reapply during the day. The AAD notes that UVA passes through window glass, and advises reapplying about every two hours outdoors and after swimming or sweating, and using about a teaspoon for the face.[3] The FDA says sunscreen should be applied about 15 minutes before exposure, that commonly missed areas include the ears, lips, back of the neck and hairline, and that it should be combined with clothing, hats, sunglasses and shade.[4]

sections.h: Why sun protection matters for appearance
paras: UVB mainly affects the epidermis, while UVA reaches the dermis and damages collagen, elastin and the extracellular matrix.[1] UV also raises levels of matrix metalloproteinase enzymes that break down collagen and reduces new collagen production.[1] Visible signs of photoageing include wrinkles and uneven pigmentation around the eyes, mouth and forehead, spider veins on the nose and cheeks, lax or leathery skin, and age spots.[1]

Photoageing references list topical tretinoin as the most effective treatment, with peels, lasers, fillers and botulinum toxin as other options, and name sun protection as the key preventive measure.[1]

SPF expresses protection against burn-causing UV under standardised application of 2 mg per square centimetre, roughly 35 ml or a golf-ball-sized amount for an adult body; most people apply a quarter to a half of that amount, which lowers effective protection.[2] The AAD says SPF 30 blocks about 97 percent of UVB, higher numbers block slightly more, and no sunscreen blocks all UV.[3]

Broad-spectrum labels denote UVA protection; the FDA defined the term in rules effective around 2012, and the EU requires UVA protection of at least one-third of the SPF for its UVA seal.[2] The FDA requires products that are not broad spectrum or are below SPF 15 to carry a warning that they help prevent sunburn only, not skin cancer or early skin ageing.[4]

A 2013 Australian trial, summarised on Wikipedia, followed about 900 participants; those assigned to daily broad-spectrum sunscreen for four and a half years had smoother, more resilient skin than those who continued usual use.[2] Reviews describe sunscreen as helping prevent melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma, with weaker evidence for basal cell carcinoma.[2]

Reported adverse effects include allergic contact dermatitis, with oxybenzone and cinnamates listed as common triggers.[2] Heavy sunscreen use may reduce vitamin D synthesis, though typical use rarely causes deficiency.[2] Independent testing by Valisure found benzene in 27 percent of aerosol sunscreens tested, from propellant impurities, leading to voluntary recalls.[2] The FDA recommends against using recalled products and advises against spraying aerosol sunscreen directly on the face.[4]

In the US sunscreen is regulated as a nonprescription drug; the FDA removed PABA and trolamine salicylate from its monograph in 2021 and has requested safety data on other filters.[2][4] In the EU it is a cosmetic.[2] Hawaii banned oxybenzone and octinoxate in 2018 and Palau restricted several filters in 2020, citing coral reefs.[2]

timeline.event: H. A. Milton Blake formulates an early sunscreen using 10% tannic acid.[2]
US FDA rules define broad-spectrum labelling.[2]
Australian trial reports smoother skin after 4.5 years of daily sunscreen.[2]
